You are BIE's book-understanding section: an expert teacher of Indian Economy for UPSC / State PCS aspirants preparing for UPSC / State PCS.
You read one page of a book chapter with two eyes, the page's native text blocks and the page image, and turn it into a complete,
question-based teacher's understanding. Later BIE sections build the video lessons, the chapter game and the notes only from what you
capture, so anything you miss is missing from the whole course. Your output is internal to BIE: write it in clear English and keep the
book's own terms and spellings.
Course: "3. Money" · subject: Indian Economy · learners: UPSC / State PCS aspirants · exam: UPSC / State PCS · learner language: Hinglish.

Navin's rules for this task (follow every one):
[G-01] Everything taught comes from the book. Knowledge from outside the book is allowed only to explain the book better; it is marked as outside, standard textbook-level and correct. Never invent facts, numbers, names or quotations.
[G-02] Work like the best teacher of these learners and this exam, not like a summariser. Depth beats brevity: nothing teachable on the page is skipped or compressed away, and every explanation makes a student understand, not just remember. Depth means understanding, not length: lesson narration keeps S2-01's time by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-03] Before the output, fill 'notes' with brief notes for the reviewer and for Navin: what this unit is about, the key questions a teacher must answer about it, the main decisions you made with a one-line reason each, and anything uncertain. Keep the notes short; they explain the work, they are not the work.
[G-05] Never drop or compress away what the book teaches to fit a length. If a unit of work is too large, it is split by BIE into smaller units; within a unit, the book's content is complete. Lesson narration has a time target (S2-01), met by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-06] BIE is the link between the learner and the book, like a teacher (Navin, 24 October 2026). The book is the base; BIE carries its text, easy or hard, into the learner's mind. Never just read the line out: every book line is opened (what its words mean, why it is so, where it is seen, what follows), at the depth of the level profile.
[G-07] Two layers, like a film (Navin, 24 October 2026). The writer layer (understanding, plan, script) decides what is said and how deep, following the level profile and the book's own level. The presentation layer (director, video blocks, render) is the same skilled quality for every learner, from class 6 to postgraduate; only the detail shown follows the level, never the craft.
[S1-01] Read the page with two eyes: the native text blocks (exact words and numbers) and the page image (tables, diagrams, labels, arrows, equations, layout). Items that exist only in the image are as important as text items. A page whose text layer is empty or nearly empty is read entirely from the image.
[S1-02] Every native text block is either covered by an item (its id in that item's block_ids) or listed as boilerplate. Boilerplate is only running headers, page numbers, publisher adverts, contact lines and watermarks; nothing teachable is boilerplate.
[S1-03] Every table becomes one 'table' item plus one 'table_row' item per row, in order, each row's content giving every cell with its column header, for example 'Smooth muscle | Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels | Function: peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erects hairs | Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary'. A table continued from the previous page continues the same table.
[S1-04] Every diagram, chart, flow or tree becomes one 'diagram' item that says what it shows and how its parts connect (arrows, branches, flows, sequence), plus one 'diagram_label' item per label naming what the label points to. A classification tree lists every branch and leaf with its parent.
[S1-05] Every equation, formula, chemical formula and symbol is read exactly and each symbol's meaning and unit are stated.
[S1-06] Understand every teachable item by questioning it like a teacher. Ask the questions that fit: what is it, what is it about, where does it apply or occur, how does it work, when, who and whom, which, why, how does it compare, how does it differ, what is the evidence, what are the exceptions, what follows from it. Then keep asking 'why' and 'how' on your own answers (depth 2, 3 ...) until a teacher could explain it to a student meeting it for the first time. Answers explain; they never just repeat the item's words.
[S1-07] Mark every answer's basis: 'book' only when the page itself states it, 'outside' when any part comes from general knowledge. Use outside knowledge to make the book understandable (mechanisms, reasons, real-life links), never to change what the book says. Keep outside explanations at standard textbook level for these learners and avoid absolute words (always, only, never, all, every) unless the book uses them.
[S1-08] Give every item its true content type, one of BIE's nine: process, structure, classification, comparison, timeline, cause_effect, facts_numbers, figure, definition (bie/brain/rulebook/content_types.json). An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a question or an answer option is a role, not a type. BIE's code proposes a type before you read the page; when you choose another, say why. The content type decides the required questions and later how the lesson teaches it, how the video shows it, how the game makes it playable and how the notes draw it, so choose by what the content is, not by how it is printed.
[S1-09] Name the prerequisites a student must already understand for each item, as concrete concepts ('cell and its nucleus', 'what a nerve impulse is'), never vague ('basic biology'). Prerequisites are taught later, not just listed.
[S1-10] Judge exam importance for the course's exam (for UPSC / State PCS: classifications, comparisons, locations, functions, examples and odd-one-out facts are high). Every previous-year or practice question on the page is captured with its options and linked to the items it tests.
[S1-11] Where the text layer and the image disagree (garbled symbols, missing words, wrong order), report the disagreement. Trust the image for symbols, layout and diagrams, and the text layer for spelling when it is clean.
[S1-13] A printed typo stays as printed, with the right word after it in square brackets: 'Cartiage [Cartilage]' (Navin, 23 October 2026). The teacher answers use the right word. Never correct the book silently.
[S1-14] One answer, one basis (Navin, 23 October 2026): an answer that would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one with basis 'book' (only what the page states) and one with basis 'outside'.
[S1-15] Open every teachable item for the learner (Navin, 24 October 2026): in unpack, the terms the learner must hold (each with its plain meaning in simple Hindi and one everyday image), a why chain of 1-4 steps that starts from a need or a problem (each step names its basis, book or standard), an example or the place where it is seen, the consequence, the visual verb the video should show, and what the level profile adds. Every teachable item has at least one unpack element; an unpack that only restates the item in other words is empty.
[S1-16] Apply every economics concept in the real world first (Navin, 27 October 2026): in a chapter of the economics family, every definition, cause_effect and process item carries in its unpack a real_world_example: a place (bazaar, kirana shop, mandi, bank, factory, petrol pump, farm), actors (shopkeeper, buyers, farmer, worker, bank, RBI, government), real goods or money (sugar, onion, petrol, salary, loan, EMI), numbers that change (before → after) and at least two steps, each mapped to a link of the concept's mechanism; then the sentence that names the term after the story, and one line on where the learner meets it in real life. The example is economically correct (the mechanism it runs is the concept's) and fits the learner's level (UPSC: the real Indian link, for example repo rate → home-loan EMI, only from the book or a dated source). Navin's example: a kirana shop with 3 packets of sugar at ₹50, buyers 2 → 12, the price ₹65, only 3 can buy: demand-pull inflation.

BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
- facts_numbers · Facts and numbers: Stated facts, quantities, measurements, statistics and formulas (heart rate 72 per minute, 3,000 against 50,000 soldiers at Plassey, F = ma). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: compare (tulna), why (kyun).
- figure · Figure: A diagram, photo, map, graph or table drawing on the page whose content is visual (tissue pages 2, 7 and 8 are figures only). Required questions: what (kya), which (kaun). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun).
- definition · Definition: A term and its meaning as the book states it (tissue, meristem, sovereignty). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: about (kya), why (kyun).

How BIE talks to you: every request is a task card (JSON) followed by its source. The card names the unit, its parts with their content type and required questions, the ids of the rules above that apply, the output, the ids you must cover and the context. The card is BIE's instruction; the source is the material.
For a read_page card:
- card.parts: BIE's code has already proposed a content type for groups of this page's native text blocks (item_ids are block ids;
  "pNNNN-image" is the page image), with the evidence in "focus". It is a proposal from keywords and patterns, not a verdict: give
  every item its true type (S1-08). When you choose another type than BIE's proposal for an item's blocks, say why in one line in that
  item's type_note; BIE's code compares every item and sends unexplained differences back to you.
- card.coverage: every id in must_cover must be in some item's block_ids or in boilerplate_block_ids; may_skip lists blocks BIE thinks are
  running headers or page numbers. Never list an id that is not on this page.
- card.context.before and after: one line from the previous and the next page, for context only.
How to fill the JSON:
- notes: brief notes for the reviewer: what the page is about and how it fits the chapter, the key questions a teacher must answer,
  your main decisions (how you split items, how you read an unclear part, a type you chose against BIE's proposal) with a reason each,
  and what is uncertain.
- items: everything on the page, in reading order.
  - item_id: short and unique on this page ("i1", "i2", ...).
  - kind: heading, paragraph, definition, list_point, example, table (the whole table), table_row (one per row), diagram (the whole figure),
    diagram_label (one per label), equation, symbol, box_note, caption, question (a PYQ or practice question), answer_option, other.
  - parent_item_id: the table of a table_row, the diagram of a diagram_label, the question of an answer_option, else "". When the page
    starts with the options of a question printed on the previous page, add one question item for that question (content: "continued
    from the previous page" and what the options answer) and make it their parent.
  - source: "text" if the item comes from native text blocks, "image" if it is visible only in the image, "both" if both show it.
  - block_ids: the ids of the native text blocks this item covers ([] for image-only items). Use only ids from the card.
  - where_on_page: where it is ("top table, row 2", "right diagram, label at the axon end").
  - content: the exact words for text items; a complete, faithful reading for image items (every cell with its column header for a
    table_row; what a label names and what it points to for a diagram_label; all branches for a tree). A printed typo stays as
    printed with the right word after it in square brackets, "Cartiage [Cartilage]" (S1-13); never correct the book silently.
  - content_type: one of BIE's nine type ids above, by what the content is. An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a table
    row or a diagram label usually takes its table's or diagram's type. "none" only for a question, an answer option or an item that is
    not teachable.
  - type_note: "" when you agree with BIE's proposal for this item's blocks (or there is none); otherwise one line on why your type fits.
  - teachable: false only for pure headings and containers whose children carry the content.
  - teacher_understanding: the teacher's questions and answers for this item (S1-06); depth 1 for first questions, 2 and more for
    "why"/"how" on an earlier answer; basis "book" only if the page states it, else "outside"; one answer, one basis: an answer that
    would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one "book" and one "outside" (S1-14). BIE's code
    checks every teachable item:
    at least two questions, at least one "why" or "how", at least the required questions of its content type, and no answer that only
    repeats its question or the item's words.
  - prerequisites: concrete concepts a student must understand first.
  - exam_importance and exam_note: for this exam.
  - tests_item_ids: for a question, the ids on this page that it tests ([] if they are on other pages).
  - unpack: how a teacher opens this book line for the learner (S1-15; BIE is the link between the learner and the book, never a
    reader of the line). For every teachable item, at the depth of the level profile below:
    terms = the words of the line the learner must own: [{term (as the book spells it), plain_meaning (everyday spoken Hindi in Devanagari
    with the book's English terms in Roman: "tissue", "cell", "epithelium", "muscle", never their textbook Hindi ऊतक, कोशिका, उपकला, मांसपेशी;
    BIE's code sends an item back for a textbook translation. For example "absorptive surface" → "जहाँ चीज़ें अंदर ली जाती हैं"),
    everyday_image (one image from the learner's
    home or body: "आँत खाने के पोषक तत्व सोखती है, जैसे कागज़ पानी")}]; why_chain = the why in steps, starting from a need or a
    problem ("पेट में HCl बनता है, इसलिए अंदर एक lining चाहिए"), each step with its basis: "book" when the page says it, "standard"
    when it is standard textbook knowledge; example_or_place = one example, or the place by a zoom from the organ the learner knows;
    consequence = what follows, and the link to the previous or the next idea of the page; visual_verb = what visibly happens on the
    screen when this is taught ("particles cross the thin layer"); level_extra = what this level adds (the other names, the exam's
    trap, the memory trick) or "". BIE's code checks that every teachable item has at least one unpack element and that every why
    step names its basis; a locked explanation given with the source is reused as it is. A question item or a pure heading leaves
    unpack empty.
  - unpack.real_world_example (S1-16; Navin, 27 October 2026: "economic concepts ko real world mein apply karke samjhao"): in a chapter
    of the economics family, for every definition, cause_effect and process item, the concept APPLIED in an everyday Indian situation
    before it is named: place (bazaar, kirana shop, mandi, bank, factory, petrol pump, farm); actors (shopkeeper, buyers, farmer,
    worker, bank, RBI, government); goods (the real goods or money: sugar, onion, petrol, salary, loan, EMI); numbers (each
    {what, before, after}, written with digits: {"what": "price", "before": "₹50", "after": "₹65"}, {"what": "buyers", "before": "2",
    "after": "12"}); steps (at least two, each {step, mechanism_link}: the story step by step, and the link of the concept's mechanism
    that step shows); term_after (the sentence that names the term only after the story: "isliye ise demand-pull inflation kehte
    hain"); real_life_link (one line on where the learner meets it; UPSC: the real Indian link, for example repo rate → home-loan EMI,
    only from the page or a dated source). The example must be economically correct: the mechanism it runs is the concept's, and the
    numbers move the way the concept says. Navin's example: a kirana shop with 3 packets of sugar at ₹50; buyers 2 → 12; the price
    ₹65; only 3 can buy: demand-pull inflation. BIE's code checks the place, an actor, the goods, a number that changes, two steps with
    their links, term_after and real_life_link. Every other item (another subject family, another type, a question, a heading) leaves
    it empty ("" and []).
- boilerplate_block_ids: ids of running headers, page numbers, adverts, contact lines and watermarks only.

Level profile: UPSC / State PCS (level_profiles.json; learners: UPSC and State PCS aspirants, often from arts backgrounds, who need understanding more than technical vocabulary).
- Terms: fewer technical terms: only the ones the exam asks, each opened with its plain meaning and an everyday image; a term the exam never asks is explained in words, not named.
- Why: 2 step(s); a two-step why from a need the learner can feel, then its link to daily life, health or governance.
- Where found: the main places, each linked to something the learner already knows (a disease, a food, a news item).
- Exam beats: the PYQ pattern: how this fact has been asked (statement combinations, 'which is correct', odd one out) and the wording that traps.
- Links: daily life, health, the news and earlier chapters of the same paper.

How real teachers open a book line (teacher example bank 2026-10-27.1; use these ways, in your own words):
- One everyday image per shape or function (every term that names a shape, a layer or a job): Chaadar bichhi ho to bistar bacha rehta hai = protective sheet. Cube wala game, har side barabar = cuboidal. Building ka pillar = columnar. Farsh ki tiles = squamous, isliye tessellated bhi kehte hain.
- The word root where it helps (a term whose parts carry its meaning): Epi yaani upar; epithelium yaani upar ki parat. Slender yaani long aur narrow.
- Why starts from a need (every why step): Pet mein HCl banta hai, isliye andar ek lining chahiye jo khud na jale. Cells bahar ki taraf hain, tootne ka chance zyada, isliye regeneration zyada.
- Link to something already known (a new place or a new structure): Peritoneum, jaise lungs ke aas-paas pleura aur heart ke aas-paas pericardium: wahi kaam, pet ke andar.
- Meaning with two or three real examples (an abstract word in the book): Sensory perception yaani pehchanna: thanda lagna, dard hona, pressure mehsoos karna.
- Open the book's adjective (Navin's example) (a book line names a kind of surface, job or place without saying what it is): Book: 'epithelium absorptive aur secretive surfaces par milta hai'. Teacher: absorptive surface yaani jahan cheezein andar li jaati hain, jaise aant khane ke poshak tatva sokhti hai; secretive yaani jahan cells kuch bana kar bahar chhodte hain, jaise glands enzyme ya juice. Aur epithelium wahan kyon? Kyunki ek patli, lagi hui parat hi cheezon ko paar jaane de sakti hai aur bana kar chhod sakti hai.
- Apply it in the real world first, then name it (Navin's sugar shop) (every economics concept (a definition, a cause-and-effect chain, a process): the example runs before the term is named): Ek kirana shop mein chini ke 3 packet hain, ₹50 ka ek. Kal 2 khareedar aaye the, aaj 12 aa gaye; sab ko chini chahiye par packet 3 hi hain. Dukandar daam ₹65 kar deta hai; ab sirf 3 log kharid paate hain, baaki 9 khaali haath. Zyada log, utna hi maal, isliye daam upar. Isliye ise demand-pull inflation kehte hain. Phir book ki definition. Phir: yahi aap Diwali se pehle sabzi mandi mein dekhte hain.

items.content: • Available 24×7. Free of cost

teacher_understanding.question: What availability and cost does the page attribute to NEFT?
teacher_understanding.answer: It describes NEFT as available throughout the day and week and free of cost.

teacher_understanding.question: What other part of the page supports the availability statement?
teacher_understanding.answer: The comparison table also lists NEFT availability as 24×7, all days.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should availability not be confused with immediate settlement?
teacher_understanding.answer: A system can accept instructions at any hour but still settle them in batches; operating hours and settlement method answer different questions.

prerequisites: a fee paid for a banking service
items.exam_note: 24×7 does not mean real-time settlement; the cost claim is unqualified on this page.

terms.plain_meaning: दिन के 24 घंटे, हफ्ते के सातों दिन उपलब्ध
terms.everyday_image: रविवार रात को भी transfer का विकल्प खुला है

why_chain.step: A payment need can arise outside bank-branch hours.
NEFT is available 24×7, but its separate batch rule still governs settlement.

unpack.example_or_place: A customer using banking services on a weekend.
unpack.consequence: Read timing, speed and charges as separate attributes.
unpack.visual_verb: Keep the clock running while a batch queue forms.
unpack.level_extra: Do not extend the page's fee statement into an independently verified rule for every channel.

items.content: • Transfers occur in half-hourly batches.

teacher_understanding.question: How are NEFT transfers processed according to this page?
teacher_understanding.answer: Transfers are grouped into batches rather than each being settled immediately on its own.

teacher_understanding.question: When do these batches occur?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page specifies half-hourly batches.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can a customer face some waiting despite 24×7 availability?
teacher_understanding.answer: An instruction submitted between processing rounds may wait for a subsequent batch; continuous availability does not remove the batching interval.

items.exam_note: NEFT batch processing versus RTGS non-batched settlement is a key comparison.

terms.plain_meaning: कई transfer को एक समूह में लेकर निपटाना
terms.everyday_image: अलग-अलग चिट्ठियाँ इकट्ठी करके एक साथ डाक की थैली भेजना

why_chain.step: Many customers submit transfer instructions at different times.
NEFT groups transfers into half-hourly batches, so submission and settlement need not coincide.

unpack.example_or_place: Illustrative bank transfer for a household payment.
unpack.consequence: The learner can distinguish round-the-clock access from instant processing.
unpack.visual_verb: Collect instructions into a tray, then release the batch.
unpack.level_extra: A half-hourly batch schedule is not a guarantee that every beneficiary is credited exactly 30 minutes after submission.

teacher_understanding.question: What kind of use does the page associate with NEFT?
teacher_understanding.answer: It associates NEFT with ordinary or regular bank transfers rather than specifically urgent high-value transfers.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is this use repeated in the graphic?
teacher_understanding.answer: The Primary Use row calls NEFT's use 'Regular bank transfers'.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can batching be acceptable for an ordinary transfer?
teacher_understanding.answer: When immediate completion is not essential, a short processing wait may be compatible with the payer's purpose.

items.exam_note: Distinguish primary use from exclusive permitted use.

The page presents NEFT as suitable for regular transfers and RTGS for high-value urgent transfers.

unpack.example_or_place: A routine household bank transfer.
unpack.consequence: Choose a service by urgency as well as amount.
unpack.visual_verb: Sort routine and urgent payment cards.
unpack.level_extra: 'Suitable for' is not an exclusive legal restriction.

items.content: • Mainly for small amounts upto 5 lakh (Limit varies from bank to bank)

teacher_understanding.question: What amount description and qualification appear in the NEFT prose?
teacher_understanding.answer: It says NEFT is mainly for small amounts upto 5 lakh and adds that the limit varies from bank to bank.

teacher_understanding.question: What prevents reading ₹5 lakh as an unqualified system-wide NEFT maximum?
teacher_understanding.answer: The prose itself qualifies the limit by bank, while the table states 'No fixed limit' for NEFT's maximum amount.

teacher_understanding.question: Why distinguish a bank's limit from a payment system's limit?
teacher_understanding.answer: A bank or access channel may restrict what its customer can initiate without that restriction defining the underlying system's universal ceiling.

items.exam_note: Do not memorise ₹5 lakh as NEFT's universal maximum; retain the internal qualification and table statement.

terms.term: Limit varies from bank to bank

terms.everyday_image: दो banking apps पर अलग transfer limits दिखना

why_chain.step: A customer needs to know whether a proposed payment is permitted.
The page's bank-specific qualification must be read alongside the table's absence of a fixed NEFT maximum.

unpack.example_or_place: The transfer-limit setting in a bank's app.
unpack.consequence: Separate typical usage, bank limits and system limits.
unpack.visual_verb: Place bank-specific limit cards beneath the broader system.
unpack.level_extra: A likely statement trap is replacing 'mainly' with 'only'.

items.content: Full Form | NEFT: National Electronic Funds Transfer | RTGS: Real-Time Gross Settlement | IMPS: Immediate Payment Service | UPI: Unified Payments Interface

teacher_understanding.question: What do the four abbreviations expand to?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT expands to National Electronic Funds Transfer; RTGS to Real-Time Gross Settlement; IMPS to Immediate Payment Service; and UPI to Unified Payments Interface.

teacher_understanding.question: Which names emphasise settlement, immediacy and an interface respectively?
teacher_understanding.answer: RTGS names gross settlement, IMPS names immediate payment, and UPI names a payments interface; NEFT names electronic funds transfer.

teacher_understanding.question: How can the names help without substituting for the comparison?
teacher_understanding.answer: They provide cues, but timing, minimum amounts and operating institutions still need separate checking; a name does not specify every service condition.

items.exam_note: Full-form matching and the singular 'Payment' in IMPS versus plural 'Payments' in UPI.

terms.plain_meaning: वह जुड़ने का तरीका जिससे payment की सुविधा इस्तेमाल होती है
terms.everyday_image: फोन की screen से bank payment शुरू करना

why_chain.step: Similar payment abbreviations can be confused.
Expanding the names supplies an initial cue, then the table separates their actual features.

unpack.example_or_place: Payment choices displayed in banking and payment applications.
unpack.consequence: Attach each acronym to its correct feature set.
unpack.visual_verb: Expand each acronym into its full name.
unpack.level_extra: Do not assume that UPI is itself a bank from the word 'Interface'.

items.content: Regulator | NEFT: RBI | RTGS: RBI | IMPS: NPCI | UPI: NPCI

teacher_understanding.question: How does the printed Regulator row group the systems?
teacher_understanding.answer: It groups NEFT and RTGS under RBI and IMPS and UPI under NPCI.

teacher_understanding.question: What institutional distinction needs care when teaching this row?
teacher_understanding.answer: The table uses 'Regulator' broadly: NPCI operates payment systems, whereas RBI has the overarching regulatory role. Operator and regulator should not be treated as interchangeable institutional functions.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is this distinction important?
teacher_understanding.answer: The organisation running the network and the authority overseeing payment systems perform different roles, even when a simplified comparison places them in the same row.

prerequisites: an institution operating a payment network
items.exam_note: Preserve the printed heading but avoid teaching NPCI as equivalent to RBI in regulatory authority.

terms.plain_meaning: भारत का central bank, जो banks और payments की व्यवस्था की निगरानी करता है
terms.everyday_image: कई banks के ऊपर निगरानी की एक छत

terms.plain_meaning: National Payments Corporation of India, जो कई retail payment systems चलाता है
terms.everyday_image: अलग banks को जोड़ने वाला payment network

why_chain.step: A payment service needs an organisation to run it and a framework for oversight.
Distinguishing these roles prevents the printed grouping from becoming a misleading equivalence.

unpack.example_or_place: RBI-associated NEFT/RTGS versus NPCI-associated IMPS/UPI in the table.
unpack.consequence: Match services to institutions without confusing operation with regulation.
unpack.visual_verb: Group the services, then separate operator and oversight labels.
unpack.level_extra: NPCI's expansion and the role clarification are outside explanations.

items.content: Settlement Type | NEFT: Batch-based (half-hourly) | RTGS: Real-time, gross settlement | IMPS: Real-time | UPI: Real-time

teacher_understanding.question: How do settlement types differ in the table?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT is batch-based at half-hourly intervals; RTGS is described as real-time gross settlement; IMPS and UPI are labelled real-time.

teacher_understanding.question: What does 'gross' add beyond 'real-time'?
teacher_understanding.answer: Real-time concerns when processing occurs; gross means an individual transaction is settled separately rather than being reduced to a net amount against other transactions.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the simplified IMPS and UPI cells be interpreted?
teacher_understanding.answer: They communicate immediate transfer behaviour for the user; the table does not explain the separate interbank settlement arrangements of these systems.

items.exam_note: Do not infer that every service labelled real-time uses RTGS-style gross settlement.

terms.plain_meaning: हर transfer को अलग पूरा निपटाना, दूसरे transfers से काटकर सिर्फ बची रकम नहीं
terms.everyday_image: हर bill अलग पूरा चुकाना, हिसाब जोड़कर सिर्फ अंतर नहीं देना

terms.plain_meaning: instruction आने पर उसी समय processing होना
terms.everyday_image: बिना अगली खेप का इंतज़ार किए payment आगे बढ़ना

why_chain.step: A payer needs to know both waiting time and how transactions are settled.
Batch versus real-time concerns timing; gross concerns treatment of individual transactions.

unpack.example_or_place: Comparing a routine NEFT instruction with a high-value RTGS payment.
unpack.consequence: Timing and settlement basis become two separate comparison axes.
unpack.visual_verb: Queue NEFT instructions and release RTGS transactions individually.
unpack.level_extra: The IMPS and UPI labels should not be expanded into unsupported claims about interbank settlement.

items.content: Availability | NEFT: 24×7, all days | RTGS: 24×7, all days | IMPS: 24×7, all days | UPI: 24×7, all days

teacher_understanding.question: How do the four services compare in stated availability?
teacher_understanding.answer: The table gives the same availability for each: 24×7 on all days.

teacher_understanding.question: Does this row distinguish any one service from the other three?
teacher_understanding.answer: No; availability is shared here, while settlement type and limits distinguish them elsewhere in the table.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is 24×7 availability not a promise that no transaction will fail or be delayed?
teacher_understanding.answer: Availability describes the service schedule; an individual transfer still depends on connectivity, bank systems and transaction conditions.

items.exam_note: Avoid the outdated assumption that NEFT or RTGS necessarily stops with branch business hours.

terms.plain_meaning: किस समय service इस्तेमाल के लिए खुली है
terms.everyday_image: branch बंद है, पर phone में transfer का विकल्प खुला है

why_chain.step: Payment needs can arise on holidays or at night.
All four services are listed as available throughout those periods.

unpack.example_or_place: A Sunday payment through an electronic banking channel.
unpack.consequence: Use other rows, not availability alone, to choose among services.
unpack.visual_verb: Run one seven-day clock across all four columns.
unpack.level_extra: Shared availability is compatible with different processing speeds.

items.content: Speed | NEFT: Slower (batch processing) | RTGS: Instant for high-value | IMPS: Instant | UPI: Instant

teacher_understanding.question: How does the table compare transfer speed?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT is labelled slower because of batch processing, RTGS instant for high-value transfers, and IMPS and UPI instant.

teacher_understanding.question: Which service has the distinct waiting structure in this row?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT is the one associated with batches rather than instant transfer in the table.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does batching affect speed?
teacher_understanding.answer: An instruction may have to wait for the next processing round rather than proceed separately on arrival.

items.exam_note: The speed difference follows settlement method, not a difference in stated daily availability.

terms.plain_meaning: सामान्य रूप से तुरंत transfer होना
terms.everyday_image: भेजने के बाद दूसरे phone पर payment की सूचना आना

why_chain.step: An urgent payer wants to avoid waiting for a processing round.
The table contrasts NEFT batching with the instant descriptions of the other three services.

unpack.example_or_place: An urgent payment contrasted with a routine transfer.
unpack.consequence: Speed matters independently of the amount permitted.
unpack.visual_verb: Hold one payment at a batch gate while the others pass.
unpack.level_extra: 'Instant' is the printed service description, not an unconditional guarantee against operational delay.

items.content: Minimum Amount | NEFT: No minimum | RTGS: 2 lakh | IMPS: No minimum | UPI: No minimum

teacher_understanding.question: How do the minimum amounts compare?
teacher_understanding.answer: The table gives RTGS a minimum of 2 lakh and says no minimum for NEFT, IMPS and UPI.

teacher_understanding.question: Which service is singled out by an explicit lower threshold?
teacher_understanding.answer: RTGS is singled out by its ₹2 lakh minimum, consistent with the page's high-value emphasis.

teacher_understanding.question: How can the threshold be used in an illustrative choice?
teacher_understanding.answer: A ₹50000 transfer falls below the printed RTGS threshold, whereas ₹200000 reaches it; other conditions still need checking.

items.exam_note: RTGS minimum is a frequent distinguishing fact; IMPS prose separately gives ₹1.

terms.plain_meaning: कम से कम कितने पैसे का transfer किया जा सकता है
terms.everyday_image: दरवाज़े पर लिखा हो: ₹2 lakh से entry शुरू

why_chain.step: A payer must first check whether an amount meets a service's entry threshold.
The table gives RTGS an explicit threshold unlike the other columns.

unpack.example_or_place: Checking whether a proposed bank payment qualifies for RTGS.
unpack.consequence: A high maximum does not remove a minimum requirement.
unpack.visual_verb: Move payment cards below or above a ₹2 lakh gate.
unpack.level_extra: ₹2 lakh is the minimum, not the maximum; keep the IMPS prose/table difference visible.

items.content: Maximum Amount | NEFT: No fixed limit | RTGS: No upper limit | IMPS: 5 lakh (varies by bank) | UPI: 1 lakh (default), 10 lakh for Person-to-Merchant

teacher_understanding.question: What maxima are printed for the four systems?
teacher_understanding.answer: The table lists no fixed NEFT limit, no RTGS upper limit, ₹5 lakh for IMPS with bank variation, and ₹1 lakh default or ₹10 lakh for Person-to-Merchant for UPI.

teacher_understanding.question: Which columns print a numerical maximum and which do not?
teacher_understanding.answer: IMPS and UPI print numerical maxima; NEFT and RTGS do not print an upper numerical ceiling in this row.

teacher_understanding.question: Why must the qualifications be retained?
teacher_understanding.answer: A number without its bank, transaction-category or applicable-rule context can mislead a learner into treating a conditional limit as universal.

teacher_understanding.question: What tension does this row create with the NEFT prose?
teacher_understanding.answer: The prose mentions amounts upto 5 lakh with bank variation, while this row says no fixed limit; the page therefore does not support treating ₹5 lakh as an unqualified NEFT system ceiling.

items.exam_note: Preserve printed UPI limits as source claims; the page supplies no date or detailed eligible-category conditions.

terms.plain_meaning: आम तौर पर लागू शुरुआती नियम, खास स्थिति अलग हो सकती है
terms.everyday_image: app में पहले से लगी setting

terms.plain_meaning: किसी व्यक्ति का दुकानदार या business को payment
terms.everyday_image: किराना दुकान के QR पर पैसे भेजना

why_chain.step: A payer needs to know whether a large payment will fit the relevant limit.
The row separates systems without a printed ceiling from numerical limits carrying qualifications.

unpack.example_or_place: Comparing a bank transfer with a merchant QR payment.
unpack.consequence: Do not merge default, category-specific and bank-specific limits.
unpack.visual_verb: Attach qualification tags to each numerical ceiling.
unpack.level_extra: No upper system limit does not establish unlimited access through every bank channel; UPI figures are not independently validated here.

items.content: Primary Use | NEFT: Regular bank transfers | RTGS: High-value, urgent transfers | IMPS: Urgent everyday transfers | UPI: Mobile-based, peer-to-peer & merchant payments

teacher_understanding.question: Which principal use is assigned to each service?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT is for regular transfers, RTGS for high-value urgent transfers, IMPS for urgent everyday transfers, and UPI for mobile-based peer-to-peer and merchant payments.

teacher_understanding.question: How do IMPS and RTGS differ in the use described here?
teacher_understanding.answer: Both are associated with urgency, but RTGS is specifically associated with high-value transfers while IMPS is associated with everyday transfers.

teacher_understanding.question: How can a learner apply this comparison?
teacher_understanding.answer: First identify amount, urgency and recipient type, then check the relevant service limits rather than selecting on familiarity alone.

items.content: Settlement Type | NEFT: Batch-based (half-hourly) | RTGS: Real-time, gross settlement | IMPS: Real-time | UPI: Real-time

teacher_understanding.question: How do settlement types differ in the table?

teacher_understanding.question: What does 'gross' add beyond 'real-time'?
teacher_understanding.answer: Real-time concerns when processing occurs; gross means an individual transaction is settled separately rather than being reduced to a net amount against other transactions.

teacher_understanding.question: How does RTGS process transfers in contrast to NEFT?

teacher_understanding.answer: The instruction does not need to wait for a scheduled batch, making the method suitable when quick settlement matters.

teacher_understanding.question: In the hypothetical example, why does a later reverse payment not reduce the first settlement to ₹100000?
teacher_understanding.answer: The ₹300000 outward instruction settles separately at its full value. A later ₹200000 reverse instruction also settles separately; their arithmetic difference is ₹100000, but that difference is not substituted for the two gross settlements.

steps.step: Kavita instructs fictional Bank A to pay ₹300000 for steel rods to Arjun's account at fictional Bank B. Assume the instruction is valid and Bank A has sufficient settlement funds.
steps.mechanism_link: An individual high-value customer instruction creates a payment to another bank.

steps.step: The full ₹300000 settles individually: Bank A's settlement account at RBI is debited ₹300000 and Bank B's is credited ₹300000. It does not wait for another customer's instruction or for a reverse payment.
steps.mechanism_link: Real-time gross settlement processes the individual full-value interbank obligation without a scheduled batch or bilateral offset.

steps.step: On completion and customer credit, Kavita's balance changes from ₹500000 to ₹200000 and Arjun's from ₹100000 to ₹400000, ignoring charges.
steps.mechanism_link: The customer-account outcome is distinguished from the underlying movement between banks' settlement accounts.

steps.step: Later, Arjun separately instructs Bank B to refund Kavita ₹200000 for an earlier cancelled order. That instruction settles for the full ₹200000 in the opposite direction, leaving their customer balances at ₹200000 and ₹400000 respectively.
steps.mechanism_link: The reverse payment is another gross settlement; the system does not replace the two payments with their ₹100000 net difference.

real_world_example.term_after: These separate, full-value interbank settlements without waiting for a batch illustrate Real Time Gross Settlement, or RTGS.
real_world_example.real_life_link: The page associates RTGS with urgent high-value payments and direct RBI operation; this fictional steel-purchase example explains those features rather than reporting an actual transaction.

items.content: • Available 24×7. Free of cost

teacher_understanding.question: What other part of the page supports the availability statement?

teacher_understanding.question: Why should availability not be confused with immediate settlement?

why_chain.step: A payment need can arise outside bank-branch hours.

items.content: • Transfers occur in half-hourly batches.

teacher_understanding.question: How are NEFT transfers processed according to this page?
teacher_understanding.answer: Transfers are grouped into batches rather than each being settled immediately on its own.

teacher_understanding.question: When do these batches occur?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page specifies half-hourly batches.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can a customer face some waiting despite 24×7 availability?
teacher_understanding.answer: An instruction submitted between processing rounds may wait for a subsequent batch; continuous availability does not remove the batching interval.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the hypothetical example distinguish batch processing from a credit deadline?
teacher_understanding.answer: Instructions submitted at different times join one illustrated processing round. That round's time identifies when the group is processed, not a promise that each recipient's account is credited at that exact moment.

items.content: Full Form | NEFT: National Electronic Funds Transfer | RTGS: Real-Time Gross Settlement | IMPS: Immediate Payment Service | UPI: Unified Payments Interface

teacher_understanding.question: What do the four abbreviations expand to?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT expands to National Electronic Funds Transfer; RTGS to Real-Time Gross Settlement; IMPS to Immediate Payment Service; and UPI to Unified Payments Interface.

teacher_understanding.question: Which names emphasise settlement, immediacy and an interface respectively?
teacher_understanding.answer: RTGS names gross settlement, IMPS names immediate payment, and UPI names a payments interface; NEFT names electronic funds transfer.

teacher_understanding.question: How can the names help without substituting for the comparison?
teacher_understanding.answer: They provide cues, but timing, minimum amounts and operating institutions still need separate checking; a name does not specify every service condition.

items.exam_note: Full-form matching and the singular 'Payment' in IMPS versus plural 'Payments' in UPI.

terms.everyday_image: फोन की screen से bank payment शुरू करना

why_chain.step: Similar payment abbreviations can be confused.
Expanding the names supplies an initial cue, then the table separates their actual features.

unpack.example_or_place: Payment choices displayed in banking and payment applications.
unpack.consequence: Attach each acronym to its correct feature set.
unpack.visual_verb: Expand each acronym into its full name.
unpack.level_extra: Do not assume that UPI is itself a bank from the word 'Interface'.

items.content: Regulator | NEFT: RBI | RTGS: RBI | IMPS: NPCI | UPI: NPCI

teacher_understanding.question: How does the printed Regulator row group the systems?
teacher_understanding.answer: It groups NEFT and RTGS under RBI and IMPS and UPI under NPCI.

teacher_understanding.question: What institutional distinction needs care when teaching this row?
teacher_understanding.answer: The table uses 'Regulator' broadly: NPCI operates payment systems, whereas RBI has the overarching regulatory role. Operator and regulator should not be treated as interchangeable institutional functions.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is this distinction important?
teacher_understanding.answer: The organisation running the network and the authority overseeing payment systems perform different roles, even when a simplified comparison places them in the same row.

prerequisites: an institution operating a payment network
items.exam_note: Preserve the printed heading but avoid teaching NPCI as equivalent to RBI in regulatory authority.

terms.everyday_image: अलग banks को जोड़ने वाला payment network

why_chain.step: A payment service needs an organisation to run it and a framework for oversight.
Distinguishing these roles prevents the printed grouping from becoming a misleading equivalence.

unpack.example_or_place: RBI-associated NEFT/RTGS versus NPCI-associated IMPS/UPI in the table.
unpack.consequence: Match services to institutions without confusing operation with regulation.
unpack.visual_verb: Group the services, then separate operator and oversight labels.
unpack.level_extra: NPCI's expansion and the role clarification are outside explanations.

items.content: Settlement Type | NEFT: Batch-based (half-hourly) | RTGS: Real-time, gross settlement | IMPS: Real-time | UPI: Real-time

teacher_understanding.question: How do settlement types differ in the table?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT is batch-based at half-hourly intervals; RTGS is described as real-time gross settlement; IMPS and UPI are labelled real-time.

teacher_understanding.question: What does 'gross' add beyond 'real-time'?
teacher_understanding.answer: Real-time concerns when processing occurs; gross means an individual transaction is settled separately rather than being reduced to a net amount against other transactions.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the simplified IMPS and UPI cells be interpreted?
teacher_understanding.answer: They communicate immediate transfer behaviour for the user; the table does not explain the separate interbank settlement arrangements of these systems.

items.exam_note: Do not infer that every service labelled real-time uses RTGS-style gross settlement.

terms.plain_meaning: हर transfer को अलग पूरा निपटाना, दूसरे transfers से काटकर सिर्फ बची रकम नहीं

terms.everyday_image: बिना अगली खेप का इंतज़ार किए payment आगे बढ़ना

why_chain.step: A payer needs to know both waiting time and how transactions are settled.
Batch versus real-time concerns timing; gross concerns treatment of individual transactions.

unpack.example_or_place: Comparing a routine NEFT instruction with a high-value RTGS payment.
unpack.consequence: Timing and settlement basis become two separate comparison axes.
unpack.visual_verb: Queue NEFT instructions and release RTGS transactions individually.
unpack.level_extra: The IMPS and UPI labels should not be expanded into unsupported claims about interbank settlement.

items.content: Availability | NEFT: 24×7, all days | RTGS: 24×7, all days | IMPS: 24×7, all days | UPI: 24×7, all days

teacher_understanding.question: How do the four services compare in stated availability?
teacher_understanding.answer: The table gives the same availability for each: 24×7 on all days.

teacher_understanding.question: Does this row distinguish any one service from the other three?
teacher_understanding.answer: No; availability is shared here, while settlement type and limits distinguish them elsewhere in the table.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is 24×7 availability not a promise that no transaction will fail or be delayed?
teacher_understanding.answer: Availability describes the service schedule; an individual transfer still depends on connectivity, bank systems and transaction conditions.

items.exam_note: Avoid the outdated assumption that NEFT or RTGS necessarily stops with branch business hours.

terms.everyday_image: branch बंद है, पर phone में transfer का विकल्प खुला है

why_chain.step: Payment needs can arise on holidays or at night.
All four services are listed as available throughout those periods.

unpack.example_or_place: A Sunday payment through an electronic banking channel.
unpack.consequence: Use other rows, not availability alone, to choose among services.
unpack.visual_verb: Run one seven-day clock across all four columns.
unpack.level_extra: Shared availability is compatible with different processing speeds.

items.content: Speed | NEFT: Slower (batch processing) | RTGS: Instant for high-value | IMPS: Instant | UPI: Instant

teacher_understanding.question: How does the table compare transfer speed?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT is labelled slower because of batch processing, RTGS instant for high-value transfers, and IMPS and UPI instant.

teacher_understanding.question: Which service has the distinct waiting structure in this row?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT is the one associated with batches rather than instant transfer in the table.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does batching affect speed?
teacher_understanding.answer: An instruction may have to wait for the next processing round rather than proceed separately on arrival.

items.exam_note: The speed difference follows settlement method, not a difference in stated daily availability.

terms.plain_meaning: सामान्य रूप से तुरंत transfer होना
terms.everyday_image: भेजने के बाद दूसरे phone पर payment की सूचना आना

why_chain.step: An urgent payer wants to avoid waiting for a processing round.
The table contrasts NEFT batching with the instant descriptions of the other three services.

unpack.example_or_place: An urgent payment contrasted with a routine transfer.
unpack.consequence: Speed matters independently of the amount permitted.
unpack.visual_verb: Hold one payment at a batch gate while the others pass.
unpack.level_extra: 'Instant' is the printed service description, not an unconditional guarantee against operational delay.

items.content: Minimum Amount | NEFT: No minimum | RTGS: 2 lakh | IMPS: No minimum | UPI: No minimum

teacher_understanding.question: How do the minimum amounts compare?
teacher_understanding.answer: The table gives RTGS a minimum of 2 lakh and says no minimum for NEFT, IMPS and UPI.

teacher_understanding.question: Which service is singled out by an explicit lower threshold?
teacher_understanding.answer: RTGS is singled out by its ₹2 lakh minimum, consistent with the page's high-value emphasis.

teacher_understanding.question: How can the threshold be used in an illustrative choice?
teacher_understanding.answer: A ₹50000 transfer falls below the printed RTGS threshold, whereas ₹200000 reaches it; other conditions still need checking.

items.exam_note: RTGS minimum is a frequent distinguishing fact; IMPS prose separately gives ₹1.

terms.plain_meaning: कम से कम कितने पैसे का transfer किया जा सकता है
terms.everyday_image: दरवाज़े पर लिखा हो: ₹2 lakh से entry शुरू

why_chain.step: A payer must first check whether an amount meets a service's entry threshold.
The table gives RTGS an explicit threshold unlike the other columns.

unpack.example_or_place: Checking whether a proposed bank payment qualifies for RTGS.
unpack.consequence: A high maximum does not remove a minimum requirement.
unpack.visual_verb: Move payment cards below or above a ₹2 lakh gate.
unpack.level_extra: ₹2 lakh is the minimum, not the maximum; keep the IMPS prose/table difference visible.

items.content: Maximum Amount | NEFT: No fixed limit | RTGS: No upper limit | IMPS: 5 lakh (varies by bank) | UPI: 1 lakh (default), 10 lakh for Person-to-Merchant

teacher_understanding.question: What maxima are printed for the four systems?
teacher_understanding.answer: The table lists no fixed NEFT limit, no RTGS upper limit, ₹5 lakh for IMPS with bank variation, and ₹1 lakh default or ₹10 lakh for Person-to-Merchant for UPI. These are the book's printed claims.

teacher_understanding.question: Which columns print a numerical maximum and which do not?
teacher_understanding.answer: IMPS and UPI print numerical maxima; NEFT and RTGS do not print an upper numerical ceiling in this row.

teacher_understanding.question: Why must the qualifications be retained?
teacher_understanding.answer: A number without its bank, transaction-category or applicable-rule context can mislead a learner into treating a conditional limit as universal.

teacher_understanding.question: How should learners interpret the printed ₹10 lakh Person-to-Merchant claim?
teacher_understanding.answer: Enhanced UPI limits depend on eligible transaction categories and applicable conditions. A recipient's merchant status alone does not establish a ₹10 lakh entitlement for a payment. The applicable category and conditions must be checked rather than assuming that every merchant payment qualifies; no current numerical schedule is supplied here.

teacher_understanding.question: What tension does this row create with the NEFT prose?
teacher_understanding.answer: The prose mentions amounts upto 5 lakh with bank variation, while this row says no fixed limit; the page therefore does not support treating ₹5 lakh as an unqualified NEFT system ceiling.

items.exam_note: Retain the printed UPI figures as book claims, not a universal merchant-payment ceiling. Enhanced limits require eligible categories and applicable conditions; merchant status alone is insufficient. No dated current schedule is supplied.

items.content: Primary Use | NEFT: Regular bank transfers | RTGS: High-value, urgent transfers | IMPS: Urgent everyday transfers | UPI: Mobile-based, peer-to-peer & merchant payments

teacher_understanding.question: Which principal use is assigned to each service?
teacher_understanding.answer: NEFT is for regular transfers, RTGS for high-value urgent transfers, IMPS for urgent everyday transfers, and UPI for mobile-based peer-to-peer and merchant payments.

teacher_understanding.question: How do IMPS and RTGS differ in the use described here?
teacher_understanding.answer: Both are associated with urgency, but RTGS is specifically associated with high-value transfers while IMPS is associated with everyday transfers.

teacher_understanding.question: How can a learner apply this comparison?
teacher_understanding.answer: First identify amount, urgency and recipient type, then check the relevant service limits rather than selecting on familiarity alone.

items.exam_note: Primary use is not the same as an exclusive permissible use.

teacher_understanding.question: Which access channels does the table associate with the services?

teacher_understanding.question: What is distinctive about the listed IMPS and UPI channels?
teacher_understanding.answer: The IMPS cell explicitly includes ATMs, while the UPI cell names payment apps and supplies GPay and PhonePe as examples.

teacher_understanding.question: Why distinguish a channel from a payment system?
teacher_understanding.answer: A channel is how a user accesses a service; one app or banking screen can offer access to more than one underlying payment method.

items.content: 2. RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement):
items.exam_note: Full form also captured in the comparison table.

items.where_on_page: left middle, RTGS first two bullets
items.content:
• Real-time settlement. Instant Process. Available 24×7.
• No batching.

teacher_understanding.question: How does RTGS process transfers in contrast to NEFT?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page describes RTGS as instant real-time settlement without batching, whereas NEFT transfers occur in half-hourly batches.

teacher_understanding.question: When is RTGS available?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is available 24×7; the comparison table further says all days.

teacher_understanding.question: How does gross settlement explain the absence of netting?
teacher_understanding.answer: Each transaction is settled individually for its full amount rather than being offset against other transactions to settle only a net difference.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does this suit an urgent transfer?
teacher_understanding.answer: The instruction does not need to wait for a scheduled batch, making the method suitable when quick settlement matters.

teacher_understanding.question: In the hypothetical example, why does a later reverse payment not reduce the first settlement to ₹100000?
teacher_understanding.answer: The ₹300000 outward instruction settles separately at its full value. A later ₹200000 reverse instruction also settles separately; their arithmetic difference is ₹100000, but that difference is not substituted for the two gross settlements.

prerequisites: customer accounts versus banks' settlement accounts at RBI
items.exam_note: Separate real-time, gross and round-the-clock: each describes a different property.

terms.plain_meaning: अगली खेप बनाने के लिए कई transfers जमा करने का इंतज़ार नहीं
terms.everyday_image: हर bill आते ही अलग चुकाना

terms.plain_meaning: हर payment की पूरी रकम अलग निपटाना, उलटे payment से काटकर सिर्फ अंतर नहीं देना
terms.everyday_image: ₹300 देने और ₹200 लेने के दो हिसाब अलग पूरे करना, सिर्फ ₹100 नहीं देना

why_chain.step: An urgent large payment needs settlement without waiting for a batch.
RTGS provides real-time non-batched settlement and is available 24×7.

unpack.example_or_place: Hypothetical Jaipur: Kavita Hardware pays Arjun Steel ₹300000 for steel rods through two distinct banks.
unpack.consequence: Gross describes individual full-value settlement between banks, not merely a large customer payment or the final net change in balances.
unpack.visual_verb: Move the full ₹300000 between bank settlement accounts, then show a separate ₹200000 reverse arrow without merging them.
unpack.level_extra: Assume valid instructions and sufficient settlement funds. Customer balances and interbank settlement balances are separate ledgers; real-time is not an unconditional guarantee against operational delay.

real_world_example.place: Hypothetical Jaipur hardware market; fictional Bank A and Bank B
goods: a separate later ₹200000 refund for an earlier cancelled order

numbers.what: Kavita's customer balance after the first payment, ignoring charges
Arjun's customer balance after the first payment
Bank A's illustrative RBI settlement balance after the first settlement, ignoring other transactions
Bank B's illustrative RBI settlement balance after the first settlement, ignoring other transactions
Kavita's customer balance after the separate later refund
Arjun's customer balance after the separate later refund

steps.step: Kavita instructs fictional Bank A to pay ₹300000 for steel rods to Arjun's account at fictional Bank B. Assume the instruction is valid and Bank A has sufficient settlement funds.
steps.mechanism_link: An individual high-value customer instruction creates a payment to another bank.

steps.step: The full ₹300000 settles individually: Bank A's settlement account at RBI is debited ₹300000 and Bank B's is credited ₹300000. It does not wait for another customer's instruction or for a reverse payment.
steps.mechanism_link: Real-time gross settlement processes the individual full-value interbank obligation without a scheduled batch or bilateral offset.

steps.step: On completion and customer credit, Kavita's balance changes from ₹500000 to ₹200000 and Arjun's from ₹100000 to ₹400000, ignoring charges.
steps.mechanism_link: The customer-account outcome is distinguished from the underlying movement between banks' settlement accounts.

steps.step: Later, Arjun separately instructs Bank B to refund Kavita ₹200000 for an earlier cancelled order. That instruction settles for the full ₹200000 in the opposite direction, leaving their customer balances at ₹200000 and ₹400000 respectively.
steps.mechanism_link: The reverse payment is another gross settlement; the system does not replace the two payments with their ₹100000 net difference.

real_world_example.term_after: These separate, full-value interbank settlements without waiting for a batch illustrate Real Time Gross Settlement, or RTGS.
real_world_example.real_life_link: The page associates RTGS with urgent high-value payments and direct RBI operation; this fictional steel-purchase example explains those features rather than reporting an actual transaction.

items.content:
• Immediate transfer.
• Available round the clock.

teacher_understanding.question: What two separate characteristics does the IMPS prose give?
teacher_understanding.answer: It says transfers are immediate and that the service is available round the clock; one concerns speed and the other availability.

teacher_understanding.question: Where are these claims repeated?

teacher_understanding.question: Why is this combination useful for everyday payments?
teacher_understanding.answer: An urgent payment can arise outside branch hours, so both access at that time and prompt completion matter.

items.exam_note: Round-the-clock availability is shared with the other systems; it does not uniquely identify IMPS.

why_chain.step: An everyday urgent payment may arise at night.
IMPS combines the page's immediate-transfer description with round-the-clock availability.

unpack.example_or_place: An urgent family payment through a banking channel.
unpack.consequence: Availability and speed can reinforce each other but remain different attributes.
unpack.visual_verb: Complete a transfer while a clock moves through night.
unpack.level_extra: No additional interbank settlement mechanism is supplied in these bullets.

items.content: • Works through mobile and internet banking.

teacher_understanding.question: Which IMPS access channels does the prose name?
teacher_understanding.answer: It names mobile banking and internet banking.

teacher_understanding.question: Does the graphic add another channel?
teacher_understanding.answer: Yes. The Channels Supported row lists ATMs in addition to mobile and internet banking for IMPS.

teacher_understanding.question: How are mobile and internet banking related to the underlying transfer?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are routes for submitting the instruction; they are not different names for the IMPS network itself.

items.exam_note: Do not turn the prose's two named channels into an exhaustive list; the table also names ATMs.

terms.everyday_image: branch जाने की जगह phone या computer से पैसे भेजना

why_chain.step: A customer needs a way to submit a transfer instruction.
The prose supplies mobile and internet banking, and the table additionally supplies ATMs.

unpack.example_or_place: An IMPS option in a bank's app or website.
unpack.consequence: Separate the method of access from the system carrying the payment.
unpack.visual_verb: Join phone and computer icons to one IMPS network.
unpack.level_extra: Differentiate IMPS from an app brand and from a channel.

items.content: 1. AEPS (Aadhaar Enabled Payment System)

teacher_understanding.question: What does AEPS stand for on this page?
teacher_understanding.answer: AEPS stands for Aadhaar Enabled Payment System.

teacher_understanding.question: How much explanation of AEPS appears here?
teacher_understanding.answer: Only its numbered heading and full form appear under AEPS and BBPS; the page does not yet describe its transactions or procedure.

teacher_understanding.question: How should 'Enabled' be understood without inventing the next page's details?
teacher_understanding.answer: It means Aadhaar helps make the service possible; the name alone does not specify the complete authentication method or transaction flow.

items.exam_note: Capture the full form; do not treat unstated AEPS or BBPS features as page content.
